prompt: What is the most general reaction of aldehydes and ketones?

choices.text: Nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl group
Electrophilic addition to the C=O bond
choices.why: The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic, so it is attacked by a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

choices.text: S_N2 substitution at the carbonyl carbon
choices.why: Aldehydes and ketones have no leaving group on the carbonyl carbon. A nucleophile adds to the C=O bond instead.

choices.text: Elimination to form an alkene
choices.why: Elimination isn't the general reaction of carbonyl compounds; nucleophilic addition is.

explanation: The most general reaction of aldehydes and ketones is the nucleophilic addition reaction: a nucleophile forms a bond to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide ion intermediate.

prompt: As a nucleophile adds to a carbonyl group, how does the hybridization of the carbonyl carbon change?

choices.text: From sp2 to sp3
From sp3 to sp2
choices.why: That's the reverse. The planar carbonyl carbon is sp2 and becomes tetrahedral, sp3, in the alkoxide intermediate.

choices.text: From sp to sp2
choices.why: The carbonyl carbon starts out sp2, with three σ bonds and one π bond.

choices.text: It stays sp2 throughout
choices.why: After addition the carbon has four σ bonds in a tetrahedral intermediate, so it becomes sp3.

explanation: When the nucleophile bonds to the carbonyl carbon, the carbon rehybridizes from sp2 to sp3, an electron pair from the C=O bond moves toward the electronegative oxygen, and a tetrahedral alkoxide ion intermediate is produced.

prompt: What intermediate forms when a negatively charged nucleophile adds to an aldehyde or ketone?

choices.text: A tetrahedral alkoxide ion
A planar carbocation
choices.why: The carbonyl carbon gains a bond from the nucleophile; it doesn't lose one to become a carbocation.

choices.text: A carbanion on the carbonyl carbon
choices.why: The electron pair from the C=O π bond moves onto the electronegative oxygen, not onto carbon.

choices.text: A carbon radical
choices.why: The reaction moves electron pairs, not single electrons.

explanation: An electron pair from the C=O bond moves toward the electronegative oxygen as the nucleophile bonds to carbon, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide ion intermediate. Protonation of the alkoxide by addition of acid then gives an alcohol.

prompt: At about what angle to the plane of the carbonyl carbon's sp2 orbitals does a nucleophile approach the carbonyl group, in degrees?
explanation: The nucleophile approaches the carbonyl group at an angle of about 75° to the plane of the carbonyl carbon's sp2 orbitals (Figures 19.4.1 and 19.4.3). As it bonds, the carbon rehybridizes from sp2 to sp3 and an alkoxide ion forms.

prompt: A neutral nucleophile that adds to an aldehyde or ketone usually carries what feature?

choices.text: A hydrogen atom that can later be eliminated, as in :Nu–H
A positive charge on the nucleophilic atom
choices.why: A neutral nucleophile has no charge. It uses a lone pair to bond to the carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: A metal atom such as Mg or Li
choices.why: The section's neutral nucleophiles, such as water, alcohols, ammonia and amines, contain no metal.

choices.text: A halogen that can later leave as a halide ion
choices.why: The section's neutral nucleophiles carry a hydrogen, not a halogen leaving group.

explanation: The nucleophile can be negatively charged (:Nu−) or neutral (:Nu). If it's neutral, it usually carries a hydrogen atom that can subsequently be eliminated, :Nu–H. Water, alcohols, ammonia and amines are examples.

prompt: Which of these is one of the neutral nucleophiles the section lists?

choices.text: Ammonia, NH3
Cyanide ion, CN−
choices.why: Cyanide is a negatively charged nucleophile.

choices.text: Hydride ion, H−
choices.why: Hydride is a negatively charged nucleophile.

choices.text: Alkoxide ion, RO−
choices.why: An alkoxide ion carries a negative charge. The neutral counterpart is an alcohol, ROH.

explanation: The section's negatively charged nucleophiles include hydroxide, hydride, carbanion, alkoxide and cyanide ions. Its neutral nucleophiles are water, alcohols, ammonia and amines.

prompt: In the second general pathway of nucleophilic addition, how does a product with a C=Nu double bond form?

choices.text: The carbonyl oxygen is protonated and eliminated as HO− or H2O
The nucleophile is protonated and eliminated as H–Nu
choices.why: If the nucleophile left, the starting carbonyl compound would re-form. In this pathway the oxygen leaves, and Nu stays double-bonded to carbon.

choices.text: A hydride ion is expelled from the carbonyl carbon
choices.why: The tetrahedral intermediate of an aldehyde or ketone doesn't usually expel hydride. The group that leaves is the former carbonyl oxygen.

choices.text: The alkoxide is protonated to give an alcohol as the final product
choices.why: That's the first pathway, which ends at an alcohol and has no C=Nu double bond.

explanation: Nucleophilic additions have two general variations (Figure 19.4.2). In one, the tetrahedral intermediate is protonated by water or acid to give an alcohol. In the other, the carbonyl oxygen atom is protonated and then eliminated as HO− or H2O to give a product with a C=Nu double bond.

prompt: For what reasons are aldehydes generally more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition reactions?

choices.text: Both steric and electronic reasons
Steric reasons only
choices.why: Sterics are part of it, but aldehydes are also more electrophilic, because only one alkyl group stabilizes the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: Electronic reasons only
choices.why: Electronics are part of it, but an aldehyde is also less hindered, with only one relatively large substituent on the carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: Neither; ketones are the more reactive compounds
choices.why: The section states the reverse: aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones.

explanation: Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones for both steric and electronic reasons. An aldehyde has only one relatively large substituent on the carbonyl carbon while a ketone has two (Figure 19.4.3), and an aldehyde's carbonyl group is more polarized.

prompt: What is the electronic reason that aldehydes are more reactive than ketones toward nucleophiles?

choices.text: Only one alkyl group stabilizes the δ+ charge on an aldehyde's carbonyl carbon
Two alkyl groups push electrons onto an aldehyde's carbonyl carbon
choices.why: An aldehyde has one alkyl group on its carbonyl carbon; a ketone has two. More alkyl groups make the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic.

choices.text: The aldehyde C=O bond is less polarized than the ketone C=O bond
choices.why: It's the reverse: aldehyde carbonyl groups are more polarized.

choices.text: The aldehyde hydrogen withdraws electrons strongly from the carbonyl carbon
choices.why: The difference is that a ketone has a second alkyl group stabilizing the positive charge, which an aldehyde lacks.

explanation: Electronically, aldehydes are more reactive because their carbonyl groups are more polarized. Just as a primary carbocation is less stable than a secondary one, an aldehyde has only one alkyl group inductively stabilizing the partial positive charge on its carbonyl carbon rather than two, so it is a bit more electrophilic and more reactive than a ketone.

prompt: The section compares aldehydes and ketones with carbocations. Which statement matches its comparison?

choices.text: An aldehyde is like a primary carbocation: one alkyl group stabilizes its positive charge
An aldehyde is like a secondary carbocation: two alkyl groups stabilize its positive charge
choices.why: An aldehyde has one alkyl group on its carbonyl carbon, not two.

choices.text: A ketone is like a primary carbocation: one alkyl group stabilizes its positive charge
choices.why: A ketone has two alkyl groups on its carbonyl carbon, like a secondary carbocation.

choices.text: A ketone is like a tertiary carbocation: three alkyl groups stabilize its positive charge
choices.why: A ketone's carbonyl carbon carries two alkyl groups, not three.

explanation: A primary carbocation is higher in energy and more reactive than a secondary one because only one alkyl group stabilizes its positive charge. In the same way, an aldehyde has only one alkyl group stabilizing the partial positive charge on its carbonyl carbon, while a ketone has two, so the aldehyde is more electrophilic and more reactive.

prompt: By the section's reasoning, which compound should be most reactive toward nucleophilic addition?

choices.text: Propanal, CH3CH2CHO
Acetone, CH3COCH3
choices.why: Acetone is a ketone, with two alkyl groups on its carbonyl carbon: more hindered and less electrophilic than an aldehyde.

choices.text: 3-Pentanone, CH3CH2COCH2CH3
choices.why: 3-Pentanone is a ketone, so it is less reactive than an aliphatic aldehyde.

choices.text: Benzaldehyde, C6H5CHO
choices.why: Aromatic aldehydes are less reactive than aliphatic aldehydes, because the ring's electron-donating resonance makes the carbonyl less electrophilic.

explanation: Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones for steric and electronic reasons, and aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde are less reactive than aliphatic aldehydes. So the aliphatic aldehyde propanal is the most reactive of these.

prompt: Why is benzaldehyde less reactive in nucleophilic addition than aliphatic aldehydes?

choices.text: The aromatic ring's electron-donating resonance effect makes the carbonyl group less electrophilic
The aromatic ring withdraws electrons by resonance and makes the carbonyl carbon more positive
choices.why: Then benzaldehyde would be more reactive. The ring donates electrons by resonance, and the carbonyl carbon is less positive.

choices.text: Benzaldehyde has two large substituents on its carbonyl carbon, like a ketone
choices.why: Like any aldehyde, benzaldehyde has one carbon substituent and one hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: Benzaldehyde has no hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon
choices.why: Benzaldehyde is an aldehyde, C6H5CHO, so it does have a –CHO hydrogen.

explanation: Aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde are less reactive than aliphatic aldehydes because the electron-donating resonance effect of the aromatic ring makes the carbonyl group less electrophilic.

prompt: Electrostatic potential maps of formaldehyde and benzaldehyde are compared. How does the carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde look?

choices.text: Less positive (less blue) than in formaldehyde
More positive (more blue) than in formaldehyde
choices.why: The aromatic ring donates electrons by resonance, so benzaldehyde's carbonyl carbon is less positive, not more.

choices.text: Negative (red), like the carbonyl oxygen
choices.why: The carbonyl carbon is still electrophilic, just less positive than in formaldehyde.

choices.text: Exactly the same as in formaldehyde
choices.why: The ring's electron-donating resonance effect makes a visible difference: benzaldehyde's carbonyl carbon is less blue.

explanation: Comparing electrostatic potential maps of formaldehyde and benzaldehyde shows that the carbonyl carbon atom is less positive (less blue) in the aromatic aldehyde. The ring's electron-donating resonance effect makes the carbonyl group less electrophilic.

prompt: p-Nitrobenzaldehyde and p-methoxybenzaldehyde are compared in nucleophilic addition reactions. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: p-Nitrobenzaldehyde is more reactive, because the electron-withdrawing nitro group polarizes the carbonyl group
p-Methoxybenzaldehyde is more reactive, because the methoxy group polarizes the carbonyl group
choices.why: The more reactive compound is p-nitrobenzaldehyde. Its nitro group is electron-withdrawing, which makes the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic.

choices.text: p-Nitrobenzaldehyde is more reactive, because the nitro group donates electrons to the carbonyl carbon
choices.why: Electron donation makes a carbonyl group less electrophilic, as the ring's donation does in benzaldehyde. The nitro group withdraws electrons.

choices.text: They react at the same rate, because both are aromatic aldehydes with para substituents
choices.why: Ring substituents change how polarized the carbonyl group is, so these two aldehydes differ in reactivity.

explanation: p-Nitrobenzaldehyde is more reactive toward nucleophilic additions than p-methoxybenzaldehyde. The electron-withdrawing nitro group polarizes the carbonyl group, making the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic (Exercise 19.4.2).

prompt: Cyclohexanone is treated with cyanide ion, and the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is then protonated. What is the product?

choices.text: A cyclohexane ring with –OH and –C≡N on the same carbon
A cyclohexane ring with –OH and –C≡N on neighboring carbons
choices.why: Cyanide bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and that same carbon's oxygen becomes the –OH group.

choices.text: Cyclohexanone with a –C≡N group on carbon 2
choices.why: Cyanide adds to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, not to the neighboring carbon, and the C=O group is used up.

choices.text: Cyclohexanol, C6H11OH
choices.why: Cyclohexanol would come from adding hydride. Here the nucleophile is cyanide, so a C≡N group ends up on the carbon.

explanation: Cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon to give a tetrahedral alkoxide ion, and protonation gives a cyanohydrin. For cyclohexanone, the product has –OH and –C≡N on the same ring carbon (Exercise 19.4.1).
